query: Our ecommerce store is profitable but runs out of cash when buying inventory. How should we forecast supplier payments and the funding gap?

cards.title: Forecast inventory funding gaps with a monthly cash bridge
cards.summary: Separate units-sold profit from supplier-payment timing to find when an ecommerce store needs cash.
cards.use_when: You have an order and inventory forecast and need to quantify the funding gap before committing to a launch or a scaling plan.
steps: Forecast net sales and COGS for units sold; inventory purchases do not automatically become that month's COGS.
Build a cash schedule from opening cash plus customer receipts, less supplier deposits and balances, fulfillment, ads, overhead, taxes, capital spending and financing payments.
Add financing proceeds separately; reconcile closing cash to the next month's opening balance.
If starting from net income instead, adjust for non-cash items and working capital; do not subtract inventory cash twice.
Identify the lowest closing cash and add a reserve for slower sell-through, delayed payouts and higher returns.
caveats: The source's example shows months where total profit is slightly positive while cash is deeply negative — profit and cash diverge whenever you prepay inventory.
This model excludes taxes, returns and payment processing unless you add rows for them.

cards.title: Why inventory purchases make a profitable store run out of cash
cards.summary: Buying stock in large lumps hits cash in the purchase month while the cost only reaches the P&L when goods sell, so profitable periods can coincide with cash shortages.
cards.use_when: Planning inventory replenishment or a seasonal stock buy for an ecommerce store, or explaining why a high-revenue month did not improve the bank balance.
steps: Compare units-sold COGS with inventory purchased and supplier payment dates.
Track deposits, balances due, inventory receipts and payables to explain cash timing.
An inventory balance increase is not automatically an equal cash payment; supplier credit and prepayments change the bridge.
Forecast cash at planned reorder dates and stress-test slower sell-through.
caveats: The case study numbers are illustrative of one store's model, not benchmarks for expected inventory turns or margin levels.
Inventory dynamics will differ by model — made-to-order, dropship or pre-order stores carry very different cash timing.
cards.source_name: Understanding Free Cash Flow for eCommerce Startups _ Finance Case Study.docx

cards.title: Cash conversion cycle explains why ecommerce can't scale arbitrarily fast
cards.summary: CCC (DIIO + DSO − DPO) plus supplier lead time and payment terms caps real growth speed regardless of ad efficiency.
cards.use_when: Setting growth targets, planning purchase orders, or evaluating whether rapid ad-spend scaling is fundable
steps: Formula: cash conversion cycle = days inventory outstanding + days sales outstanding − days payable outstanding.
Work through the compounding: if $50 gross profit lets you buy 11 units next cycle and yields $55, which buys 12, inventory purchasing grows only incrementally off prior gross profit.
Add supplier lead time — e.g., a 90-day lead time with full upfront payment means you must fund inventory 90 days before selling it, potentially forcing a 90-day stockout while waiting for cash.

Levers to fix it: negotiate better supplier terms (e.g., only 20% upfront, paying the balance on shipment — the source's example reduces stockout from 90 days to ~20), reduce lead time via a different manufacturer, or use inventory financing.
Compare financing cost, repayment timing, guarantees and collateral in actual quotes; stress-test slower sales before borrowing.
caveats: The source describes spend rising from $20k to $200k per month, a tenfold increase, with substantial inventory financing; this is an anecdote, not a benchmark.
Growth capacity depends on working capital, supplier terms, lead times and margins; no universal annual growth ceiling follows from this example.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Build a Mini Cash Flow Statement to Find Working Capital Needs and Runway
cards.summary: Reconcile net income with inventory purchases to project real cash burn and how much capital the store must raise.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much funding or cash buffer the store needs and when, especially for inventory-heavy CPG or subscription-box businesses.
steps: In a simplified bridge, start with net income, add back inventory COGS expensed, then subtract all actual inventory supplier cash payments, whether goods have sold or not.
Add other non-cash and working-capital adjustments separately. Do not also subtract inventory/payables movements already captured by the supplier-payment bridge.
Add any starting capital (source scenario begins with $500k raised) and roll the cash balance month by month.
Expect cash to be choppier than net income: the source's example shows cash going negative around month 8 and again needing a large inventory outlay shortly after.

Use the trough of the cash curve to size the raise: in the source's example, the business needed roughly $1-1.5M cumulative to reach profitability even though operating income turned positive earlier.
Separately note the store's revenue run rate (last month's revenue x 12) as a real-time pacing metric alongside trailing 12-month actuals, and be explicit which one you quote.
caveats: This mini cash flow ignores other assets and liabilities by design — it is not a full three-statement model.
Capital need figures are the source's scenario and depend heavily on lead times, payment terms and growth rate.

cards.title: Sequence the forecast from marketing spend forward
cards.summary: Forecast ecommerce financials by starting with marketing budget, converting it to orders via CAC, then deriving inventory and cash needs.
cards.use_when: You are building a financial model for a new ecommerce or Amazon FBA business and need to know how much inventory and cash to line up.
steps: Start with the marketing budget line by month — the source's example began at $1,000, rose to $1,500, then increased $1,000/month out to month 16.
Apply CAC to convert spend into expected new orders (source example CAC: $41 per order).
Translate orders into units of inventory needed, remembering you must purchase inventory well in advance — the source notes checks of $10,000–$50,000 for stock before any revenue.
Model cash timing explicitly: inventory is paid for before Amazon or customers pay you, so the model must show when cash goes out versus comes in.
Add a cohort/LTV layer to show when paid orders turn profitable through organic sales and repeat purchases.
Use Excel hygiene as the source does: freeze panes on months and cost categories so assumptions stay visible as you build across months.
caveats: The marketing budget trajectory and $41 CAC are source examples, not projections.
Cash timing is the main risk in FBA businesses — the source highlights large upfront inventory payments as the core challenge.

query: How does discounting a $100 product to $70 with $60 variable costs change break-even CAC and ROAS?

cards.title: Treat discount and CAC as one acquisition cost pool
cards.summary: Discounts and marketing spend are mathematically equivalent per-customer costs, so combine them into a single budget and optimize the split for total profit, not per-customer margin.
cards.use_when: Planning next quarter's promotional calendar and ad budget, or deciding whether a deeper discount or more ad spend will grow profit for the whole store.
steps: Build the scenario grid with the same ad spend in every column, then vary the discount. Source case: $100,000 spend, $1.50 per click blended, ~66,667 sessions in all scenarios, undiscounted price $200, COGS $75 ($50 product + $25 fulfillment).

Convert discount into a conversion-rate assumption. Source assumptions: 0% discount → 1.5% website conversion → 1,000 purchases → $100 CAC; $30 discount → 2.2% → 1,433 purchases → $70 CAC; $60 discount → 3.8% → 2,500 purchases → $40 CAC.

Compute contribution margin post-CAC per customer for each scenario. In the source, all three land at $25 per customer, because discount plus CAC totals $100 in every scenario: 0% + $100, $30 + $70, $60 + $40.

Now total it up across the whole business. Source results: scenario A $200,000 sales, $125,000 pre-marketing contribution, $25,000 post-marketing; scenario B $243,000, $136,000, $36,000; scenario C $350,000, $162,000, $63,000. The deepest-discount scenario produced the most total profit in this particular case.
Do not assume the deepest discount always wins. The source states it can go both ways: some brands make more money by shrinking revenue with spectacular unit economics on a smaller base of customers.

Reframe your planning as one pool: 'we will spend $X this year on demand creation — how do we split it between discounts and ad platforms to maximize sales and profit?' Treat the discount line and the marketing line as two forms of the same cost of acquisition.

Prefer attaching your best discounts to a loyalty or subscription on-ramp rather than a flash sale. The source argues flash-sale converters often will not buy without a big discount, while customers who join a loyalty or subscription program have self-selected into higher lifetime value.
Run this as a future-strategy split test with identical spend before committing to the deeper discount calendar.
caveats: The 1.5%/2.2%/3.8% conversion lifts and the $1.50 CPC are assumptions illustrating the method, not measured benchmarks.
Deep discounting can damage brand — the source explicitly says it is not advocating discounting 'like crazy'.
The result is highly sensitive to whether the assumed conversion lift from discounting actually materializes; if it does not, the deeper-discount scenario loses money.

cards.title: Model discounts and CAC as one combined acquisition cost
cards.summary: A discount and paid acquisition are mathematically equivalent spend per customer — add them together to see true cost of acquisition.
cards.use_when: You are choosing between a deeper discount and more ad spend to drive first purchases and want to compare them on equal footing.
steps: Define the unit economics of one customer: net AOV (after discount) − COGS = contribution margin; then subtract CAC = contribution margin post-marketing.
Run a scenario table with identical ad spend across scenarios (source example: $100,000 each, $1.50 per click, 66,667 sessions, $200 list price, $75 COGS).
Vary the discount (0%, $30, $60) and set an assumed conversion-rate lift for each (source's illustrative assumptions: 1.5% → 2.2% → 3.8%).
Compute purchases, CAC (= ad spend ÷ purchases) and contribution margin post-marketing for each scenario.

In the source's example all three scenarios land at exactly $25 contribution margin post-marketing per customer because discount + CAC totalled $100 in each — the discount is not automatically worse than the ad spend.
Use this to decide allocation: the discount and the ad budget are two ways to spend the same acquisition dollar, and the split is a choice, not a fixed rule.
caveats: The conversion lifts and $100 discount+CAC equality are the presenter's constructed example, not a universal result — real conversion lift depends on your price point, audience and offer.
Discount depth can damage brand perception and reference prices over time; the source cautions against discounting indiscriminately.

cards.title: Recalculate contribution and break-even acquisition cost before discounting
cards.summary: Model discounted net revenue against all variable order costs before setting acquisition targets.
cards.use_when: Pricing and offer decisions — planning a promo, a bundle, a gift-with-purchase, or a clearance push, and setting the media efficiency target that promo must hit.
steps: Calculate pre-ad contribution per order as net revenue less landed product cost, fulfillment, payment fees and expected return costs, without double-counting discounts or refunds.
With $100 net revenue and $60 variable costs, contribution is $40; break-even CAC is $40 and revenue ROAS is 100/40 = 2.5.
At $70 discounted net revenue and unchanged $60 costs, contribution is $10: break-even CAC is $10 and ROAS is 70/10 = 7.
Compare a bundle or gift-with-purchase using actual basket costs and measured incremental conversion; a $4 gift does not guarantee another $100 sale.
Check clearance cash recovery separately from profitable ongoing acquisition.
caveats: Break-even here excludes fixed overhead and target profit; set a lower operating CAC ceiling.
Shipping, fees and returns can change with the offer; use store-specific assumptions.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Fix CAC measurement before setting CAC targets
cards.summary: Use total ad spend divided by new customers, and pair CAC against first-purchase gross profit on new customers only.
cards.use_when: Setting acquisition targets, reviewing agency performance, or diagnosing why a 'healthy' blended CAC is not producing profit.
steps: Calculate CAC as total advertising spend over the period divided by total new customers acquired in that period — not platform CPA, which runs on attributed numbers and typically flatters the result.
Refuse channel-level CAC breakdowns; the source argues attribution makes per-channel deltas unreliable.
Pair CAC against gross profit on first purchase, not blended AOV times a possibly-wrong gross margin percentage. New customers typically have lower AOV and heavier discount-driven front-end offers.

Worked check: a $100 blended AOV at an assumed 70% gross margin looks like $70 GP and a comfortable $35 CAC — but if the new-customer AOV is really $90 and front-end discounting compresses margin, true first-purchase GP might be $50, making the CAC target wrong.
Answer 'what is a good CAC?' as a non-question: a $100 CAC against $10,000 first-order GP is excellent; a $100 CAC against $20 GP is a loss. Judge CAC only relative to first-purchase gross profit.
caveats: Attribution-free CAC is a deliberate simplification; channel decisions then rely on experiments such as geo-lift.
Requires clean new-versus-returning customer tagging in your platform and analytics.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Calculate CAC payback from cohorts, not from flat monthly gross profit
cards.summary: Dividing CAC by a single month's gross profit ignores churn; real payback must sum declining cohort gross profit until cumulative profit covers CAC.
cards.use_when: Deciding how fast a subscription or replenishment offer repays acquisition spend before scaling the media budget.
steps: Estimate payback the naive way first to see the size of the error: source example takes $28 monthly gross profit against $90 CAC and reports 3.2 months.
Layer in retention by order: source high-churn cohort of 3,500 buyers retained 100% at order one, 75% at order two and 50% at order three, with most customers gone by order 18.
Multiply CAC by the full original cohort count to get total marketing outlay — 3,500 × $90 = $315,000 in the source example.
Sum gross profit across periods using each period's surviving customer count, then find when cumulative gross profit crosses total CAC. Source high-churn example breaks even around month 8, not 3.2.

Repeat for a lower-churn cohort: source software-style example retained 45% at 12 months and 15% at 24 months, breaking even around month 9 against a 7.1-month naive estimate — roughly a 27% error versus roughly 150% in the high-churn case.
Scenario-test CAC itself: the source notes a move from $125 to $225 CAC shifted breakeven from about month 5 to about month 11.
caveats: The source warns payback is 'almost always' calculated incorrectly and that errors typically make real payback 20–100% (sometimes 200%) longer than reported.
Source numbers are worked examples, not universal benchmarks; rates vary by category and retention curve.
If your subscription allows skipping or irregular order frequency, count payback in number of orders rather than months.

query: How should an ecommerce store allocate inbound freight and duties to SKU landed cost and COGS?

cards.title: Capture freight and duty against the right purchase order at the time it happens
cards.summary: Stop accumulating unattributed freight and duty invoices; attach each cost to the purchase it belongs to so landed cost can actually be calculated.
cards.use_when: When inbound logistics costs are piling up unallocated, or when setting up the purchasing workflow for a growing ecommerce operation.
steps: When raising a purchase order, record the agreed unit price and verify it against the supplier invoice that later hits the financials.
At the moment a freight or duty invoice arrives, identify which purchase order(s) it relates to and record the cost against them — do not file it to be sorted out later.
Avoid the common failure mode the source describes: a growing pile of freight and duty invoices never matched back to the products they belong to.
When one shipment carries multiple products, allocate the total freight or duty across them, weighting where the cost differs by unit (bulk, weight or value).
Treat this as a people-and-process discipline first; software helps execute it but does not replace defining who captures what and when.
caveats: Spreadsheets can work at small scale, but the source advises inventory management software as the business scales and allocations become weighted.
Specific inventory-management or accounting apps are mentioned in the source as vendor material; verify current features and integrations before selecting one.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Separate inbound inventory freight from customer delivery costs
cards.summary: Document the cost's economic purpose and accounting policy, then include variable selling and delivery costs in ecommerce contribution analysis.
cards.use_when: Setting up the chart of accounts or reviewing shipping cost treatment for an ecommerce store that ships physical products to customers.
steps: Identify what the charge purchases: inventory, customer delivery, support, referral or another service.
Use the applicable accounting policy for statutory classification rather than a universal label from another business model.
Track the charge separately per order or channel where possible.
Reconcile gross profit to contribution after variable fulfillment, commissions and support costs before setting CAC limits.
caveats: Service and software examples in the source do not establish universal COGS rules for a physical-product store.

cards.title: Move from spreadsheets to weighted landed-cost allocation as SKU count grows
cards.summary: Attribute lump-sum freight and duty down to unit level so every SKU shows a true cost, using software once manual weighting becomes unreliable.
cards.use_when: When you sell many SKUs per shipment and cannot tell whether individual products are profitable, or when preparing to scale purchasing.
steps: Recognise the problem shape: costs arrive as lump sums (one container, one duty invoice) but decisions are made per SKU.
Choose an allocation basis — the source notes you may have ordered three or four different items and the freight or duty needs to be weighted differently across them.
Do the weighting consistently for every shipment; inconsistent bases across months make margin trends meaningless.
Move to inventory management software when volume or SKU count makes spreadsheet weighting error-prone, so landed cost is computed automatically per item.
Verify that the software's output ties back to the actual freight and duty invoices you received before relying on the margins it reports.
caveats: The source flags a vendor relationship behind this recommendation; treat it as a capability requirement, not a specific product endorsement.
No specific trigger volume for switching from spreadsheets is given — judge it by error rate and time cost, not a fixed number.
cards.source_name: Calculating COGS_ What Ecommerce Businesses Get Wrong.docx

cards.title: Separate dropship product and shipping costs in margin analysis
cards.summary: Compare dropship and stocked orders on complete order contribution, with a documented accounting policy.
cards.use_when: When calculating margin for a drop-shipped product line, or when deciding whether to offer free shipping on a SKU.
steps: Separate supplier product charges, inbound costs where relevant and customer-delivery charges.
Document how bundled supplier invoices are allocated and reported under the applicable policy.
Do not let free versus separately charged shipping alone determine accounting classification.
Include all merchant-paid delivery costs when comparing order contribution for stocked and dropship products.
Reconcile internal contribution reporting with the accountant's inventory and expense classifications.
caveats: Presented as a general rule with explicit exceptions, not a universal standard; confirm treatment with your accountant for statutory accounts.
Deciding whether to negotiate freight or find suppliers sits outside this method — that is a sourcing decision.

cards.title: Calculate true gross margin with the "all in until it's in" COGS rule
cards.summary: Define COGS as every cost incurred to get a product onto the warehouse shelf ready to sell, so gross margin reflects reality rather than guesswork.
cards.use_when: When setting product prices, deciding which sales channels to sell on, or reviewing whether a SKU is actually profitable.
steps: Identify purchase and attributable inbound/conversion costs that bring inventory to its present location and condition; not every incremental cost qualifies.
Include supplier purchase price less applicable discounts, inbound freight and non-recoverable duties under the accounting policy.
Allocate shared inbound costs across SKUs using a documented driver such as weight, volume or value.
Carry qualifying costs in inventory until the goods are sold, then recognize the related COGS.
Recalculate landed unit cost when supplier prices, exchange rates or freight change.
caveats: The source is an accounting practitioner's guidance for statutory reporting; different KPIs such as contribution margin may be more useful internally than statutory COGS for some decisions.
Manufacturers have an additional layer of cost above simple bought-in goods; the walkthrough assumes a buy-and-resell model.

context:
[366fbbf40de61633c337b152] Capture freight and duty against the right purchase order at the time it happens
Use when: When inbound logistics costs are piling up unallocated, or when setting up the purchasing workflow for a growing ecommerce operation.
- When raising a purchase order, record the agreed unit price and verify it against the supplier invoice that later hits the financials.
- At the moment a freight or duty invoice arrives, identify which purchase order(s) it relates to and record the cost against them — do not file it to be sorted out later.
- Avoid the common failure mode the source describes: a growing pile of freight and duty invoices never matched back to the products they belong to.
- When one shipment carries multiple products, allocate the total freight or duty across them, weighting where the cost differs by unit (bulk, weight or value).
- Treat this as a people-and-process discipline first; software helps execute it but does not replace defining who captures what and when.
Caveat: Spreadsheets can work at small scale, but the source advises inventory management software as the business scales and allocations become weighted.
Caveat: Specific inventory-management or accounting apps are mentioned in the source as vendor material; verify current features and integrations before selecting one.

[0f57ba17ebb21ce64a32f5e1] Separate inbound inventory freight from customer delivery costs
Use when: Setting up the chart of accounts or reviewing shipping cost treatment for an ecommerce store that ships physical products to customers.
- Identify what the charge purchases: inventory, customer delivery, support, referral or another service.
- Use the applicable accounting policy for statutory classification rather than a universal label from another business model.
- Track the charge separately per order or channel where possible.
- Reconcile gross profit to contribution after variable fulfillment, commissions and support costs before setting CAC limits.
Caveat: Service and software examples in the source do not establish universal COGS rules for a physical-product store.

[427dd537598d6dd51796775a] Move from spreadsheets to weighted landed-cost allocation as SKU count grows
Use when: When you sell many SKUs per shipment and cannot tell whether individual products are profitable, or when preparing to scale purchasing.
- Recognise the problem shape: costs arrive as lump sums (one container, one duty invoice) but decisions are made per SKU.
- Choose an allocation basis — the source notes you may have ordered three or four different items and the freight or duty needs to be weighted differently across them.
- Do the weighting consistently for every shipment; inconsistent bases across months make margin trends meaningless.
- Move to inventory management software when volume or SKU count makes spreadsheet weighting error-prone, so landed cost is computed automatically per item.
- Verify that the software's output ties back to the actual freight and duty invoices you received before relying on the margins it reports.
Caveat: The source flags a vendor relationship behind this recommendation; treat it as a capability requirement, not a specific product endorsement.
Caveat: No specific trigger volume for switching from spreadsheets is given — judge it by error rate and time cost, not a fixed number.

- Reconcile internal contribution reporting with the accountant's inventory and expense classifications.
Caveat: Presented as a general rule with explicit exceptions, not a universal standard; confirm treatment with your accountant for statutory accounts.
Caveat: Deciding whether to negotiate freight or find suppliers sits outside this method — that is a sourcing decision.

query: How do subscription churn and contribution per shipment determine lifetime value and an affordable CAC?

cards.title: Compute Subscription Lifetime Orders from Monthly Churn
cards.summary: Estimate lifetime subscription orders from billed periods, order frequency and contribution per shipment.
cards.use_when: Comparing subscriber versus one-time-buyer value to decide how hard to push subscription conversion and how much you can afford to spend acquiring subscribers.
steps: Estimate churn for the store's actual billing period; the source's 25% monthly churn is an illustration.
Expected active periods are 1/churn in a constant-churn model. Orders equal active periods times orders per period; four periods mean four orders only with one shipment each period.
Multiply expected orders by contribution per shipment after discounts, fulfillment and returns.
Compare observed subscription and one-time-purchase cohorts, including acquisition cost and cash payback.
Blend cohort values only with matching acquisition cohorts and realistic subscription conversion rates.
caveats: 1/churn assumes a constant churn rate over the customer's life, which rarely holds exactly.
Subscribers often carry a lower contribution margin per order (bigger discount) even though lifetime value is higher — model both margin and lifetime, not just one.

cards.title: Calculate customer lifetime value from churn and gross margin
cards.summary: Estimate subscription contribution LTV using consistent monthly purchase frequency, margin and churn, then validate against observed cohorts.
cards.use_when: You are setting a CAC ceiling for a subscription or repeat-purchase store and need to know how much you can afford to spend to acquire one customer.
steps: Use monthly orders per active customer, net AOV, explicitly defined contribution rate and monthly customer churn.
Under constant monthly churn c, expected billed periods are approximately 1/c for customers active at the first bill.
Illustration: $25 AOV x 60% contribution x 1.35 orders per active month / 22% monthly churn = about $92 contribution LTV.
A $92 CAC would consume all modeled lifetime contribution before overhead, time value and risk; set a lower ceiling with a payback constraint.
Check monthly cohort cash contribution and observed repeat orders; do not apply subscription churn mechanically to non-subscription purchases.
caveats: LTV is most important for subscription or repeat-purchase businesses; it matters less for one-time-purchase categories.
The formula is only as good as the churn assumption — using an early, high-churn cohort understates LTV, and a mature cohort may overstate it for new traffic.

cards.title: Spend above first-order profit when LTV justifies it
cards.summary: A subscription can profitably spend more on acquisition than the first order returns because later months repay the CAC.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to scale paid acquisition on a subscription product even though first-order economics look unprofitable.
steps: Compute first-order contribution: AOV × gross margin (example: $25 × 60% = $15) versus your CAC.
If CAC is higher than first-order contribution, check whether cumulative gross profit across the average lifetime exceeds CAC.
Use the cohort view: month 0 has 986 transactions, month 1 has 986 × (1 − churn), and each month's revenue × gross margin accumulates.
In the source's example, even spending $50 to acquire a customer whose first order only nets $15 works, because the average 4.5-month lifetime repays it and adds profit.
For hyper-growth planning, use historical churn rates to predict the payback period (the source cites roughly one year to profitability at very high growth rates) before committing ad budget.
Investors evaluating the business will ask for LTV before funding growth spend — keep the cohort calculation current.
caveats: This only works if churn is stable and measured; if churn worsens as you scale into colder traffic, the payback promise breaks.
The example numbers are illustrative, not benchmarks.

cards.title: Derive customer lifetime value per cohort in three columns
cards.summary: Cumulative lifetime revenue divided by the original cohort size, multiplied by gross margin, gives the LTV you should actually set CAC against.
cards.use_when: Setting the maximum allowable customer acquisition cost for a subscription or replenishment offer, or stress-testing a media plan's breakeven.
steps: Build cumulative lifetime revenue per cohort by adding each month's revenue to the running total. Source example: a cohort buying $1,750 in month zero reached $14,000 cumulative by month 11.
Divide cumulative revenue by the locked original cohort headcount to get average cumulative revenue per acquired customer — source example: $406 per customer across 35 customers.
Multiply by gross margin to get LTV. Source assumption used 65% gross margin, turning $406 of revenue into roughly $264 of lifetime gross profit.
Sanity-check the first-purchase view: in the source example a customer initially spent $50 with only $33 of gross profit against a $115 CAC, so month-one economics alone look impossible.
Trace the crossover month by month — source example reached $65 cumulative gross profit by purchase two, $95 by purchase three and $123 by purchase four, surpassing the $115 CAC there.
Use the resulting LTV to set the CAC ceiling and to justify spend that looks unprofitable on the first order.
caveats: The source's $50/month, 65% margin, $115 CAC figures are illustrative modeling assumptions, not benchmarks.
Gross margin here excludes marketing and overhead — do not substitute net margin or the payback math breaks.

cards.title: Convert churn into average customer lifetime with 1/churn
cards.summary: Average customer lifetime equals 1 divided by the churn rate over the same period, which lets you compare monthly and annual subscriptions on one scale.
cards.use_when: Comparing payback and LTV scenarios across subscription plans, renewal frequencies or box programs when you need a common lifetime figure in months.
steps: Under constant churn per billing period, expected active billed periods are approximately 1/churn, including the first active period.
At 25% monthly churn this is four monthly periods; multiply by orders per active period to estimate orders.
An annual renewal model with 40% annual churn gives 2.5 annual billed periods; it is not identical to a monthly cancellation model.
Compare plans using their actual billing and cancellation schedules and observed cohort revenue.
Treat lower churn as a scenario to validate, not guaranteed permission to increase CAC.
caveats: This is a simplified constant-churn model; it assumes a steady churn rate and does not capture cohort-to-cohort quality differences.
The source's churn bands (25% down to 5% monthly) are illustrative scenarios, not benchmarks for a given store or category.
